sentences.text: Aragosaurus was a large, quadrupedal herbivore that lived during the early Berriasian, approximately 145 to 140 million years ago, in Galve, Teruel, Spain.
This animal reached a length of about 18 meters and weighed approximately 25 tonnes.
It possessed large, wide teeth adapted for slicing leaves and branches from tall conifer trees.
Aragosaurus ischiaticus is the only known species of this extinct sauropod genus, a macronarian that lived in Europe.
Like its relative Camarasaurus, Aragosaurus had spatulate teeth ornamented with longitudinal grooves.
The species name A. ischiaticus refers to the robust pelvis, specifically the large development of the pubic process of the ischium and the mace-like expansion of the ischiatic process.
The first caudal vertebrae were robust with widened neural spines, likely serving as anchor points for ligaments that consolidated the upper region of the tail base.
Original Aragosaurus fossils are exhibited at the Paleontological Museum of Galve and in Dinópolis-Legendark.
The type species A. ischiaticus was discovered by José María Herrero Marzo in 1958.
Aragosaurus was finally described by Sanz, Buscalioni, Casanovas, and Santafé in 1987 from the El Castellar Formation in Galve, Teruel, Spain.
Aragosaurus had forelimbs shorter than its hind limbs, though not as drastically short as is common in other camarasaurids.
The femur of Aragosaurus could reach a length of 1.4 meters.
Like its relative Camarasaurus, Aragosaurus had large holes in its cervical vertebrae.
The genus Aragosaurus and the species A. ischiaticus were named by Sanz et al. in 1987.
Aragosaurus is classified within the unranked family Macronaria.
Aragosaurus was a heavy herbivore nearly 18 meters long and weighing about 20 tonnes, living in environments near the coast of the Tethys Sea.
The discovery of Aragosaurus supported the theory that all continents were once united in Pangea millions of years ago.
Close relatives of Aragosaurus lived in nearby areas like modern-day Portugal, while others lived in distant regions such as North America or East Africa.
The Paleobiology Database records the time range for Aragosaurus as Kimmeridgian to Tithonian, from 154.8 to 143.1 million years ago.
